entries.notes: Name as recorded by Claudius Ptolemy (1st–2nd century AD); identified by Azerbaijani historians with early Shamakhi.
Arabic name attested on coins minted at al-Yazidiyya from 757/8 onwards; named after Arab governor Yazid ibn Usayd.
The name Shamakhiyya appears in 9th–11th century Arabic sources alongside Yazidiyya; the older name eventually displaced the latter.
Arabic form of the city name as used in medieval Arab geographical sources.
English form of the city name, widely used in European travel accounts from the medieval period onward.
Modern Azerbaijani name of the city.

sources: 1191 earthquake so strong that Shirvan capital was moved to Baku
events.description: Powerful earthquake struck Shamakhi; Shirvan capital temporarily transferred to Baku.

sources: Ibn al-Athir 1221 capture and destruction by Mongol invaders
events.description: Shamakhi captured and destroyed by Mongol forces. Ibn al-Athir describes heroic resistance by the inhabitants. Archaeological fire layers confirm the destruction.

sources: In 1500–1501, it was taken by the Safavid dynasty
events.description: Shamakhi taken by the Safavid dynasty under Shah Ismail I in 1500–1501.

sources: 1667 earthquake worst with death toll of 80,000, one-third of city collapsed
events.description: The worst recorded earthquake at Shamakhi; death toll of 80,000 according to Persian merchants' reports; one-third of the city collapsed.

sources: In 1721, the Lezgins sacked the city. They massacred thousands of its Shia inhabitants
events.description: Lezgins of Shirvan and Dagestan, aided by Sunni inhabitants, sacked the city and massacred thousands of its Shia inhabitants, also looting property of Christian inhabitants and foreign (mostly Russian) merchants.

sources: In 1742 Shamakhi was taken and destroyed by Nader Shah of Persia
events.description: Shamakhi taken and destroyed by Nader Shah of Persia to punish inhabitants for their Sunni creed; a new town of the same name was built ~26km to the west.

sources: devastating earthquake of 1859, when the capital of the province was transferred to Baku
events.description: Devastating earthquake of 1859 led to transfer of the provincial capital from Shamakhi to Baku; the city declined sharply thereafter.

sources: last catastrophic earthquake recorded in 1902, which destroyed the 10th-century Juma Mosque
events.description: Last catastrophic earthquake recorded in Shamakhi; destroyed the 10th-century Juma Mosque.

entries.notes: Ptolemy lists Kamachia among Albanian cities. The region was part of Caucasian Albania in the early centuries CE.

The Azerbaijani source mentions the city was founded or developed under Sasanian Shah Khosrow I Anushirvan (6th century). Sasanian suzerainty over Shirvan from mid-3rd century; inferred from regional history.

Arab conquest of the Caucasus region in mid-7th century. Numismatic evidence from Shamakhi (Yazidiyya) coins from 757/8–767/8 confirm Arab administration. Inferred from regional history bridging to attested 8th-century coins.
Shamakhi served as a capital of the Shirvanshah realm from the 8th to 15th centuries. The Shirvanshah dynasty ruled the city throughout the medieval period.
Ibn al-Athir describes the Mongol capture and destruction of Shamakhi in 1221. Archaeological fire layers confirm this. City came under Mongol rule.
Shirvanshah rule reasserted after Mongol/Ilkhanid period; Shamakhi continued as Shirvanshah capital through the 14th–15th centuries.
Taken by the Safavid dynasty in 1500–1501 under Shah Ismail I. Initially Farrukh Yassar's descendants ruled under Safavid suzerainty, then fully incorporated as a Safavid province in 1538.
Russians entered Shirvan in 1723 during the Russo-Persian War but soon retired, leaving the city to the Ottomans who controlled it 1723–1735.
After Nader Shah's rise, Safavids/Afsharids recaptured the region. In 1742 Nader Shah took and destroyed Shamakhi, rebuilding it 26km west. The Afsharid state controlled the region.
After Nader Shah's death, the Shirvan Khanate emerged as a semi-independent entity ruling Shamakhi under nominal Iranian suzerainty.
The Shirvan Khanate was incorporated into the Russian Empire during the Russo-Persian War; confirmed by the Treaty of Gulistan (1813).
Following the fall of the Russian Empire, Shamakhi came under the Azerbaijan Democratic Republic (1918–1920).
Soviet takeover of Azerbaijan in 1920.
Azerbaijan declared independence from the Soviet Union in 1991.
The site is identified with Ptolemy's Kamachia, located within the cultural sphere of Caucasian Albania.
Armenian communities are attested historically in Shamakhi. Armenian presence in the broader Caucasian Albania region predates the medieval period.
Arabic became an administrative and religious language with the Arab conquest. Coins were minted with Arabic inscriptions. Administrative language until Shirvanshah reassertion.
Persian was the language of culture and administration throughout the Shirvanshah and Safavid periods. John Bell (1715) noted city elites spoke Persian.

Adam Olearius (1637) described Turkish (Azerbaijani) as the common language of all inhabitants regardless of ethnicity, used across Shirvan and Persia. John Bell (1715) confirmed Turkish was the common language.

Armenians were extensively documented in Shamakhi by multiple sources from the 16th century: Jenkinson (1562), Carmelite monks (1607), Olearius (1637), Pedro Cobro (1670s). In 1873 they were 5,177 out of ~25,000 inhabitants.
Georgians are mentioned by Olearius (1637), Pedro Cobro (1670s), and John Bell (1715) as a notable community in Shamakhi.
Russian became an administrative language after incorporation into the Russian Empire in 1805. By 1903, 3% of population was Russian.
Islam spread to the Caucasus with the Arab conquest in the 7th century. The Friday Mosque is attested archaeologically from the 8th–9th centuries.
Christian communities (Armenians, Georgians) are attested in Shamakhi from the medieval period onward. Likely present from earlier given Caucasian Albanian Christianity.
Shirvanshah realm was predominantly Sunni Muslim. By the 8th–10th century the Islamic character of the city is well established.
Generic Islam entry closed when Sunni/Shia distinction becomes apparent from the 8th century onward.
The Safavid dynasty imposed Shia Islam as the state religion after 1500. The 1721 massacre targeted the Shia population specifically.
Sunni population remained, noted in sources including the 1721 Lezgin attack supported by Sunni inhabitants. In 1903, 22% of the Muslim population was Sunni.
Armenians were a significant community in Shamakhi throughout the Safavid and later periods, documented by multiple sources from 1562 onward. In 1873 they numbered 5,177 out of ~25,000.
Russian presence from 1805 brought Eastern Orthodox Christians. By 1903, about 3% of population was Russian.

First mentioned as 'Kamachia' by Ptolemy (1st–2nd century AD); Khinisli archaeological site 2km west suggests ancient settlement. Treating as a town by the early centuries CE based on Ptolemy's mention among Albanian cities.
Served as capital of the Shirvanshah realm from around the 8th to 15th centuries. Archaeological layers confirm 8th–9th century urban occupation.
Capital of Shirvan province under the Safavid Empire from 1538 onward.
Destroyed by Nader Shah in 1742; new town built 26km west; old town later rebuilt and continued as a regional centre under the Shirvan Khanate and later Russian Empire.
After the 1859 earthquake, the provincial capital was moved to Baku; Shamakhi declined in importance but remained an inhabited town.

Venetian diplomat Giosafat Barbaro (1476) described the city as having 'four to five thousand houses'. Using the figure as a rough indicator only; actual population not given. NOT converting houses to people — figure omitted as a strict count. Recorded only as a qualitative indicator of size.
Sources state the population of Shamakhi in the mid-1700s was about 60,000, described as one of the best and most populous cities of Persia. Majority were Armenians according to the source.
Encyclopædia Britannica stated 25,087 inhabitants in 1873: 18,680 Tartars and Shachsevans, 5,177 Armenians, 1,230 Russians.
Brockhaus and Efron Encyclopedic Dictionary (1903): 20,008 inhabitants (10,450 males, 9,558 females); 3% Russians, 18% Armenians, 79% Azerbaijani Tatars.
